title: M3-A2 + M3-D1 — declare the MCP elicitation capability and its handler in ONE commit
wave: M3 wave 3 (plan lines 7347-7360; the harness mislabels this range as M2 — it is M3)
one_line: omp starts answering elicitation/create from MCP servers with a real multi-field form, and decline / cancel / timeout each arrive at the server as a different answer on the wire.
user_visible_effect: A spec-compliant MCP server can now ask the user a question mid-session and get a real answer back. Before this, the server never even asks, because omp never advertised the capability in the initialize handshake. After this, it asks, the user sees a form in the composer area, and choosing 'decline' is reported to the server as decline rather than as an empty submission. The flip side is deliberate: declaring the capability without a handler would make every probing server receive -32601, which is strictly worse than silence — so the two halves must land together.

test_contract:
Two externally observable contracts, and each has a consumer who breaks visibly if it regresses.

(1) THE GATE. An MCP server must not be able to elicit unless omp advertised the capability, and when omp HAS advertised it, the same request must be answered. Consumer: the MCP server itself. If the gate is missing, servers start asking a client that cannot answer; if the handler is missing, servers that ignore the gate receive -32601, which is strictly worse than the current silence. The negative half is the one that makes the half-shipped state fail a suite instead of passing review: a manager with no handler installed must return -32601 for a forced `elicitation/create`, and the fixture must report `sent: false` when the capability was absent from the initialize params.

(2) THE THREE-WAY OUTCOME. decline, cancel, and timeout must each arrive at the server as a different, distinguishable value. Consumer: the server, which typically branches on the action. A regression that collapses decline into an empty submission is invisible to a user and is the exact protocol bug this item exists to prevent, so it must be asserted at the wire, not on a returned boolean. Additionally: a `required` property blocks submit; a `writeOnly` property is masked in the render AND its value never appears in the transcript; and a handler that throws surfaces as a JSON-RPC error rather than an unhandled rejection.

Both contracts are exercised through a real MCPManager and a real stdio transport against a spawned fixture server, not through a locally re-implemented shape. `packages/coding-agent/test/mcp-roots-list.test.ts` is explicitly NOT the model here — it declares in its own comments that it does not exercise the wiring.

effort: L, ~5 days as a single indivisible unit. A2 (the capability declaration) is genuinely a few lines once the types exist. D1 is the whole cost: designing the manager->UI seam, the per-mode policy for interactive / ACP / RPC / headless, three distinct wire outcomes, sanitization of untrusted server strings, and two new test files plus a fixture. Do not split the estimate — the plan is explicit that this is the one item in M3 that should not have its budget raided to pay for something else, because getting the order wrong produces a user-visible protocol error.
risk: Shipping the capability before the handler. It is the highest-leverage change in the milestone and therefore the easiest to land alone and call done: the diff is one line in client.ts, it type-checks, and it makes omp look more capable. Every spec-compliant probing server then starts receiving -32601 from manager.ts:1039 — a visible protocol error where today it simply never asks. The second-order risk is the one the plan understates: the ACP bridge at acp-agent.ts:375 already collapses decline and cancel into `undefined`, so the obvious implementation — reuse elicitFormFromAcpClient for the ACP mode and model the interactive mode on it — silently reintroduces the exact three-way distinction the item exists to preserve. Write the outcome type first, then make every mode produce it.
open_questions: HEADLESS/SDK POLICY (plan section 10, question 10 — unanswered, and the implementer must not guess). What does omp do when an MCP server elicits in headless/SDK mode with no interactive surface? The two natural wrong answers — hang the request forever, and silently auto-decline — are both visible at the protocol layer. Recommended default to put in front of a human: auto-decline with a `logger.warn` naming the server and the request message, and make it a real `{ action: "decline" }` on the wire rather than an error — plus an opt-in programmatic handler so SDK embedders are not stuck with it. Confirm before step 13.

SECRET MARKER. Is the secret field indicated by MCP's `writeOnly: true`, by `format: "password"`, or by an omp-specific extension? The MCP spec uses writeOnly. Confirm which one the servers in the wild actually send before step 8 hard-codes it; getting this wrong means secrets render in plaintext.

ACP RE-ELICITATION. In ACP mode the manager is created per managed session (acp-agent.ts:2667) and the outbound bridge already exists. Should the handler reuse `unstable_createElicitation` verbatim, or should MCP-originated elicitations bypass the editor client and be handled locally? These are very different UXs and the plan does not say.

RPC REQUEST NAME. The exact RPC method name and payload shape for forwarding an elicitation to an RPC client is unspecified. rpc-mode.ts:600 (requestRpcEditor) is the shape to mirror, but the method name needs a decision because RPC clients key off it.

TIMEOUT. Should an elicitation form time out at all? ACP's bridge honors `dialogOptions.timeout`; the MCP request carries no timeout of its own, so this needs an explicit default (and the plan requires timeout to be a THIRD distinct wire outcome, which means the value must be chosen deliberately, not inherited as 'undefined').

plan_corrections.claim: The plan never states whether the elicitation form must queue behind other dialogs.
plan_corrections.verdict: OMISSION — a real bug waiting to happen.
plan_corrections.correction: An MCP server can elicit at any moment, including while a permission prompt or an ask dialog already owns `ctx.editorContainer`. The interactive presenter MUST be built on `ExtensionUiController.#presentDialog` (line 1281), which routes through the `#dialogActive` / `#dialogQueue` gate (lines 92-93). Presenting the form directly into `editorContainer` — the obvious thing to write — makes two surfaces fight for focus, and the loser is whichever the user was already answering.
plan_corrections.evidence: `sed -n '1281,1336p'` shows #presentDialog's queue branch (`if (this.#dialogActive) { this.#dialogQueue.push(startPresentation); } else { startPresentation(); }`); `sed -n '92,93p'` shows the two fields.
